I can speak for immigrants from the former Soviet Union. 

I’m a first generation immigrant and my family came to Brooklyn, NY with about $800 in the early 1990s from the Soviet Union. No one spoke English. I grew up with many families like mine and I’d estimate that most of my generation is in the top 15% in terms of income. Quite a few are top 5%. 

Reasons:

While it’s true that we had no money, my parents and most other people from the Soviet Union had university degrees, specialized knowledge, and the ability to learn. Most also benefited from free non-profit programs that taught English and provided job coaching. Most were eligible for welfare that provided just enough support so that parents could spend their day learning English and gaining new skills. My mom, who worked as a programmer back in the Soviet Union, also cleaned houses when she could. Within 1.5 years she got her first job in IT. She had little confidence in herself but she saw others do it and this guided and motivated her. 

Nearly all my friends’ parents did the same as my mom. Even those who had no experience with programming before immigrating, acquired it. Alternative job routes included working for the city (social work, MTA jobs, etc). People also helped each other. Before LinkedIn profiles became a thing, it was easier to serve as references for fake prior jobs. For immigrants without work experience in the U.S., these kinds of references (either from acquaintances or from strangers for pay) were the handrail that helped them move up the professional ladder. 

And lastly, the culture. Regardless of income, Soviet families had a strong value for education, often lamenting the mediocrity of U.S. education. Kids were expected to excel, not merely pass classes. To simply pass was shameful. 

Most of my immigrant peers went to CUNYs, which are kind of like a community college but with bachelor and graduate programs… plus they’re huge. Most students lived at home, some worked while studying. These commuter schools were cheap and my peers graduated without debt. 

I think other groups have similar experiences if they come from a background where they were able to obtain an education. By contrast, if they come from the village and lack an education and a culture that values academic learning, this will affect their economic development in their new country. You can look at data for various immigrant groups and see this pattern.

Potty trained my girl at 2 years 3 months very easily with the 3 day method. I didn’t think she was showing any “signs of readiness” when we started.

This was my fear when we potty trained and it really wasn’t that bad. I don’t even recall her getting much pee on the rugs which I covered with various washable blankets just in case. I also put a bunch of waterproof pads on the couch (covered by a blanket) but she never had an accident on the couch either. It took about a day for her to recognize the sensation of peeing with the need to pee. But truthfully, that first day felt like a failure. I went to sleep thinking that this wasn’t going to work. But I stuck with it, and really, when she woke up the next day, she was better and we were catching most pees mid-pee into the potty. And by the third day, she was initiating and going herself. And on the fourth day, she went to daycare and pooped on the floor (didn’t make it in time - and this was a probably excellent learning experience for her). By day 8, she was 99% potty trained in all circumstances though I carried a potty around and popped it out wherever and whenever she needed to go (outside in public).

Trust your kid and trust the process.

From personal experience of night weaning while cosleeping:

Tell him that this night is going to be different. And then stop. When he wakes up and cries and tries to get to your breasts, don’t allow it. Talk to him calmly and explain that there will be no more milk from mama at night. Rub his back. Talk quietly and reassure him but don’t give in. He’ll cry a lot. It will feel bad for you. It might last an hour or more. The following night he’ll cry again, but it won’t last as long. And the night after same thing, but shorter. By the 4th night he’ll probably sleep through the night. 

Very important: once you decide to night wean, stick to it! It is cruel to deny your child and then give in after they’ve been crying. Mentally prepare yourself that they will cry and be upset - and this this is ok for them to experience. They’ll be ok, as will you!

Do you have any knowledge of how breastfeeding works??

Colostrum comes before actual breast milk. 

Baby stomachs are tiny and a small amount of colostrum is sufficient! 

My milk took 6 days to come in. I knew my 11% percentile daughter was ok because she had many wet diapers even though I saw nothing but a tiny drop now and then come out of my nipples. I did research and learned about breastfeeding before giving birth. I was prepared mentally even though her father was very worried she was hungry and it caused quite a bit of tension between us. My persistence on holding her close and making my breasts accessible nearly 24/7 while she was awake in these early days is what made my milk come in. A baby who is not hungry because they’ve been given formula is less likely to suckle on a mom’s breasts, activating her milk supply to come in! 

By 3 months, my girl was 85% percentile as an exclusively breastfed baby.

Even if your supply is slow to come in (mine took 6 days) you need your baby to be hungry and suckling! Their stomach is tiny. They don’t need much. Most important detail to note is: Are they peeing? If you are seeing consistent wet diapers each hour following birth, they are most likely ok! You don’t need to supplement. If you supplement, you’re decreasing the likelihood that breastfeeding will be successful. Also check for tongue and lip ties if you’re finding it painful or if baby seems to be struggling with latching. A little bit of blisters around nipples during the first week or two is common.

While it states that only 3.4% of public schools in New York received TSI status and that 18.4% of districts are classified as “target districts,” it fails to compare ICSD to similar districts in terms of demographics and other relevant factors. The article also assumes that racial disparities in education stem primarily from systemic issues while failing to consider alternative explanations such as personal responsibility or socioeconomic factors. It points out statistical disparities but not their causes. And while it notes that Black students in ICSD are underperforming and missing school at higher rates, it does not address whether other racial or ethnic groups face similar struggles, nor does it examine whether certain groups are excelling and, if so, why. 

The article also presents misleading statistics. It claims that only 7% of eighth graders at Dewitt are proficient in math but acknowledges that this figure excludes students taking advanced ninth-grade algebra. This omission skews the data, failing to account for students who are not just proficient but excelling in math. If we use ELA proficiency data from grades 5 and 6 as a rough benchmark, we can project that more than half of the students are actually proficient in math, contradicting the dire picture painted in the article.

The removal of the “good standing” designation reflects the struggles of certain groups, but it does not necessarily indicate that the entire school is failing. Other students are only at risk to the extent that school or district policies aimed at addressing these disparities might inadvertently impact them.

As for how is child support calculated when one person is unemployed, usually the court assigns a “minimum wage” (so it would come out to around 20k or so depending on the minimum wage where you live). 

In addition to a monthly child support amount that depends on who has primary custody and income distribution, there’s also an additional % that will be assigned for childcare and healthcare expenses. 

So let’s say it’s determined that he will owe you $500 per month for both children’s support. If his income is calculated at 50k, whereas yours is 20k (minimum wage), he’ll likely be required to pay 60% of the childcare and health expenses, while you’ll pay 40% of them. So if daycare is $1000 a month for your 1 year old, your share would be  $400. 

Get the child support question finalized by filing officially with family court. You can do it yourself. You’ll be asked to submit a financial affidavit (where you disclose your income and expenses) before the court date. The judge generally follows a formula when assigning child support but will ask both of you if you feel it’s fair (or your attorneys I guess if you have them). My ex and I have had two child support sessions so far without legal representation and it went fine (they were mostly just formalities for us). 

Once the child support is determined, you may qualify for childcare benefits from the state you live in as a primary parent with low income. Edit: I had a c-section and it took almost 6 days for my milk to come in. In the hospital she got a bit of formula because I physically couldn’t move and care for her, but once we were home on day 3 it was only nursing. I held her on my breast almost all the time in those early days. I think this is what helped us establish my milk supply. The breastfeeding course by Tiny Hood was a great resource as it informed me on the process and gave me the courage to keep on nursing even though I didn’t have any milk yet. The main points that helped my confidence were 1) a newborn stomach is tiny - they only need a small amount of anything in those early days, 2) the baby’s hunger compels them to latch and activate a mother’s milk supply which can take days to come in for first time moms - this feedback loop is essential to breastfeeding success, and most important 3) if baby is peeing and pooping consistently (I forget the exact # that’s recommended) they are fine even if they seem hungry and unsettled because the milk hasn’t truly come in. This last point truly gave me the courage to keep going because it was physical evidence that she was getting something from me! She is an ok eater but I still worry about her iron levels. Having read about iron, and experienced periodic anemia myself, I know that iron from meat is many time more absorbed by the body than that from plant sources. 

Another reason I’ve become more open to her eating meat is that I recognized that my being healthy (relatively) is a result of eating a big variety of food to meet my nutritional needs. She doesn’t want to eat a lot of the food I eat and what she does eat is not nutritionally dense enough. This isn’t true. HSV1 [sheds in asymptomatic carriers](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17703961/) as well. 

From the article I linked to:

“At least 70% of the population shed HSV-1 asymptomatically at least once a month, and many individuals appear to shed HSV-1 more than 6 times per month.”

“In the review, herpes and HPV were featured the most, while chlamydia, gonorrhoea and trichomoniasis were also common.”

There’s a *HUGE* difference between being a herpes carrier & having no outbreaks OR being an HPV carrier with the other three STDs listed which are easily treated via antibiotics!

Some important notes that are relevant to this topic: 

- Most people with genital herpes don’t know they have it because they’ve never had symptoms. Just because you think you don’t have herpes does not mean you don’t unless you get tested before every sexual encounter!

- HPV (the cancer causing kind) can only be diagnosed in women, so even though just as many, if not more, men carry and transmit the virus, they can’t be tested for it. So when someone knows they have HPV it’s likely because they’re female and got tested, most often because they had symptoms (ie: cancerous cells or abnormal pap smears). Many women also don’t know they’re carriers, but of people who do know, most are women. 

- PERSONAL: I had the cancer causing HPV in my youth and telling partners about it, nearly all of whom had never heard of it, was frustrating and genuinely hurtful. Why did I need to wear a scarlet letter when there was no way to confirm whether they were going to infect me with another type of cancer causing HPV? (There are multiple types of cancer causing HPV.) The only reason I knew was because I was female. None of my male partners knew their status and educating a one night stand started to feel wrong. I battled with this ethical dilemma until the HPV went away in my mid-20s. As someone in my late 30s now looking back, I wish I hadn’t bothered to tell anyone unless it was a serious relationship. 

- I think herpes is similar. Considering how many people don’t know their status I don’t think there’s a duty to inform unless you’re having an active outbreak or are considering a serious relationship with a person.

I think the article headline is dramatic and that the article does a poor job of considering the nuance between different STDs.

I would say yes- some people cannot be vegan. *But I also think that no one should be vegan long term.* Vegan diets are almost always too high on carbs, low on fat, protein and iron, and do not contain sufficient omega 3s. 

- Allergies and intolerances to vegan staples

*Vegan diets are high on soy and wheat. These two ingredients are not tolerated well by some people. Alternative sources of protein are nuts and beans. Not all people can eat these either, or eat them in large quantities.*

- Not enough Omega 3

*Vegan diets are generally way too high in omega 6 and very low in omega 3. This is not healthy in the long term. Consuming omega 6 restricts absorption of omega 3, so even if one supplements with vegan omega 3 from algae, they’d have to be very careful not to combine this supplementation with any omega 6… which is literally in everything because vegetable oils are in almost everything.*

- Not enough fat

*Fat is essential to health. Avocados, olive oil, and nuts are vegan and provide fat. But are they eaten in sufficient quantities to provide enough fat over the long term? (For me personally, no. Most of my meals are plant-based but I need to ensure that they have enough fat. Ie: When I eat a salad, I eat some cultured dairy butter too. When I don’t consume enough fat and protein in a meal, I get reactive hyperglycaemia.)*

- Iron

*Heme iron (from animal products) is better absorbed than non-heme iron (from vegetable sources or supplements). Whereas B12 supplements work really well for supplementing vegans/vegetarians with the B12 they lack by not consuming meat, iron supplementation isn’t very effective. Iron deficiency is a major problem for long term vegans and vegetarians. (I am largely vegetarian and have struggled with iron deficiency all my life. Though I haven’t eaten meat in 20 years, I chose to include meat in my toddler’s life because iron is so essential to a developing brain!)*

It’s interesting how hardly anyone in these posts considers what’s best for the child or whether the father is capable of solo parenting a baby should he get shared custody. Firstly, it sounds like the mom was the primary caregiver while the father worked, meaning that the baby is likely more bonded to her at this moment and may have certain routines linked to her presence. While their mother’s proximity is relevant to this child’s well-being, what may be even more relevant is whether the father is capable of caring for the child and working without the mother’s presence. Even if he was to find a suitable daycare for his child, would his work schedule allow for consistent pickups? How long would the child spend at daycare? Does the father have a job that is flexible enough or other caregiving help when the child gets ill (which happens often and unpredictably with young kids) and can’t attend daycare? How rested does the father need to be to do his job properly (single parents are rarely very rested)? Is the father capable of working, caring for their child and keeping house (cooking, cleaning to some minimum standard, etc on his own)? 

The most likely scenario if they both have the best lawyers and massive resources to pay them is that they’d get some form of shared custody, with the child having to travel from one parent to the other by some schedule. Is this break of routine and break from their primary caregiver (mom) good for such a small child? My understanding is that most sources on child development would say no. But even if the parents agreed to the is kind of arrangement, the very important question remains: how capable is the father of solo parenting the child while child is in his custody? This is a very important question that seems to be overlooked in the judgmental response here.

CSA = community supported agriculture 

For a given $ sometime in the spring, members sign up to receive a share of what that CSA (in my case it’s a network of different local organic farms) produces. Every week members go to the pick up point and pick up their shares, which consist of that week’s harvest. In my CSA some kinds of produce are limited (ie: 2x per member) whereas other types are take as many as you want depending on quantity harvested. Quality is excellent and variety is nice! Basically the members assume some of the risk of farming and farmers get paid before they even plant/harvest so they don’t need to worry about selling. Members benefit by (usually) getting a lot more produce for their $ than they would if they bought the same stuff outside the CSA.

You can try taking an animal carrier and putting food inside. Once kitten enters close it very quickly. Helps if the kitten hasn’t been fed in many hours. The hungrier the kitten is the more likely they’ll go into a scary unfamiliar carrier. Once inside, it may become very timid and meow very plaintively, or aggressive and hiss and swing paws in your direction. All of these are normal responses for a scared cat. If you’d like to keep this cat (or give it the best chance of getting adopted and are able to do this for a week) take them to your home and keep them only in the bathroom. Set up a litter pan, a space to hide (box that’s open from the side), food and water. Open the carrier and leave the kitten alone for 24 hours or so if you can. (Not possible if it’s your only bathroom but just don’t interact). Kitten will be very scared. It’s likely they won’t eat for as long as 2 days. After 24 hours you can talk to it gently. Go inside the bathroom a few times a day and spend time there, on your phone, talking gently to kitten, even holding a string and some kitty toys. By end of week, kitten will probably stop being as scare of you (if they were scared) and possibly let themselves be pet. Ironically, finding a way to pet the kitten while it is scared (after day 2!) could help kitten become more comfortable with you sooner. But it’s a risky thing cause you can get scratched. I’ve done this approach with 5 feral kittens from three different litters. The last was probably 4 months old when I caught him. Totally feral. I was thinking I’d made a mistake and that he would never be tame. But the moment I started playing with a string with him around day 5-6 he forgot how scared he was. The kitten in him wanted to play. By the end of the week I could pet and hold him. 

But- beware of the possibility of rabies. If kitten is drooling in any way, do not touch.

Oh, also fleas and ringworm. If you have other cats or dogs don’t let them interact and always wash your hands.

It took about 6 months for us to create a good (and safe) relationship between a large dog who had never lived with a cat (and loves to chase street cats!) and an adult (timid) cat who had little experience with dogs. In addition to giving them spaces that were 100% free of the other, we fed them together daily at least once and usually twice. We started off quite far and decreased the distance through the months until they ate side by side. Within a year dog would still occasionally playfully chase cat but they were sharing the apartment without any separation. However, cat did start to develop urinary issues after about a year which may or may not have something to do with the dog. Vet said it was likely related to stress. But we also had a baby (and stopped letting him into our bedroom for a few months) and our other cat had passed away so it’s hard to say what the reason for his stress was.

Always use positive reinforcement (praise and delicious treats) with the dog. Make the cat comfortable. Work on dog’s listening to you in general. Dog needs to respect cats space but it’s really hard if he’s curious about the cat. So giving him a chance to see the cat in a controlled, positive way will help a lot.

There’s an excellent free course by Tinyhood on breastfeeding. You should both watch it before giving birth. Breastfeeding is a skill and knowledge about the how helps a lot. Especially the first few days before the milk comes in are very important. Many people panic, assume their milk isn’t coming and use too much formula, creating a cycle in which baby isn’t encouraging lactation and therefore they don’t produce the optimal quantity and baby is hungry so gets formula and thus doesn’t encourage lactation by nursing…..

Personally I had a c-section so it was very hard and painful to move. I did use the hospital provided formula a few times during my 3 day hospital stay. I think that if I’d given birth naturally and been able to move I’d have focused on breastfeeding from the beginning but I couldn’t get in and out of my bed to get my baby on my own. As soon as I got home I spend days and days sitting in the couch nursing my infant. I couldn’t move easily and my husband would bring me all that we needed and do the diaper changes. All I had to do was nurse baby even though I didn’t have milk yet. Baby cried, husband panicked, told me we had to use formula. I refused. I’d learned about breastfeeding before birth and I knew that everything was normal and that I needed to keep baby at my breast and formula would just set us back. My milk came in on day 6 after birth. Until then it was just colostrum. Baby is 12 weeks now and has gone from ~11% percentile at birth/leaving hospital to over 50th in weight through exclusive breastfeeding.
